memory_update.text: For AI, keep the map broad: demand begins with hyperscaler training and inference, but the research chain must include packaging, substrates, HBM, optics, rack power, switchgear, passives, inspection tools, and grid interconnection.
Advanced packaging/CoWoS-like capacity is a top bottleneck because capacity additions require cleanroom buildout, specialized tools, acceptance cycles, yield learning, and customer qualification.

ABF substrates and ABF film should be tracked as a high-priority hidden bottleneck beneath AI accelerators; supplier count, material allocation, qualification time, and customer advances are key indicators.

Data-center medium-voltage switchgear and electrical distribution are major AI deployment constraints; factory capacity, skilled labor, utility interconnection, and vendor expansion plans are key catalysts.
High-end AI-server MLCCs are a low-attention passive-component chokepoint; the key is the narrow high-capacitance, low-ESR/ESL product band rather than commodity MLCC demand.
Inspection and metrology tools for advanced packaging, IC substrates, and HBM/package lines can be hidden capacity gates because they protect yield and enable usable output.
Customer prepayments, co-funded capacity, qualification wins, backlog growth, and capex announcements should be treated as stronger catalysts than generic AI narrative mentions.
Custom AI accelerator and AI networking growth are catalysts that push the map beyond GPUs into networking ASICs, switches, optical links, substrates, and high-speed PCB/interconnect.

Need primary-source verification from filings, earnings transcripts, and company presentations for AI revenue mix, customer concentration, qualification status, backlog, capex timing, lead times, and utilization at each low-attention supplier.

Need to distinguish true bottleneck nodes from cyclical recovery nodes in MLCCs, PCBs, optics, OSATs, and power semiconductors by checking pricing, utilization, gross margin, and customer-specific AI order evidence.

TTMI should be tracked as an underfollowed AI advanced-PCB and ultra-HDI interconnect derivative, but survival to later layers requires primary-source proof of AI data-center revenue mix, advanced interconnect margins, customer concentration, and backlog.

4062.T remains one of the strongest ABF substrate bottleneck candidates in this chunk due to external claims around rising substrate complexity and customer advance payments, but primary financial and customer verification is required.

3037.TW should remain in the substrate watchlist as a Taiwan-listed ABF/IC substrate and PCB candidate, but current evidence is hypothesis-level without verified AI/HPC revenue mix or TSMC ecosystem exposure.

ONTO maps to the inspection/metrology yield-control gate for advanced packaging, panel-level packaging, and package substrates; the key evidence gap is whether recent orders are directly tied to AI/HPC capacity expansions.

MKSI maps to substrate and advanced PCB process-equipment demand through laser drilling, plating, chemistry, and precision processing; the key risk is confusing broad cyclical PCB recovery with AI-specific substrate expansion.
6239.TW is an underfollowed memory-backend and OSAT hypothesis for AI/HBM crowding-out and FOPLP, but needs utilization, pricing, customer, and AI/HPC validation before ranking higher.

AMKR is a reference anchor for OSAT advanced-packaging relief capacity, supported by external evidence, but its AI/HPC revenue mix, Arizona milestones, and exact constraint exposure remain evidence gaps.

CAMT maps to inspection/metrology for advanced packaging, IC substrates, HBM package lines, and high-density interconnect, but its AI linkage is still mostly inference pending customer/order-level confirmation.

COHR and LITE should be tracked as optical interconnect and InP photonics capacity names; the major evidence gaps are AI datacenter revenue mix, InP capacity constraints, backlog durability, and customer commitments.

ALMU is only a speculative shadow candidate in this funnel; do not promote without primary-source evidence of revenue materiality, customer qualifications, product readiness, and sufficient cash runway.

For every ticker in this chunk, Layer 2C should collect primary-source filings, latest earnings-call transcripts, investor presentations, segment revenue mix, capex/backlog disclosures, and customer concentration before any ranking upgrade.

Market-pricing checks are still missing for the chunk: current market capitalization, enterprise value, revenue multiple, analyst coverage count, 3/6/12-month price moves, short interest where applicable, and ownership concentration.

Falsification triggers for this chunk should include lead-time compression, customer insourcing, excess capacity additions, substrate or optical component price declines, order cancellations, lower utilization, failed qualification, margin compression, or AI capex cuts.

3189.TW and 8046.TW should remain in the underfollowed AI substrate lane, but both require primary-source verification of AI/HPC substrate materiality versus mobile, consumer, and broader PCB cyclicality.

CLS is a plausible underfollowed EMS/hardware-platform derivative of AI networking and hyperscale infrastructure demand, but the key survival test is customer/program evidence and margin contribution.
PLXS remains a weaker EMS hypothesis until filings show material AI, data-center, networking, or industrial automation program exposure.
ETN and VRT should be retained as reference anchors for the data-center power and thermal lane, not as underfollowed discoveries.

POWL is a focused underfollowed switchgear and power-control candidate whose AI relevance depends on proving data-center backlog rather than only oil/gas, petrochemical, utility, or industrial demand.

ATKR is a second-order electrical balance-of-system candidate, but its AI relationship is indirect and must be tested against construction-cycle pricing, channel inventory, and commodity input normalization.
HUBB and NVT are broad electrical infrastructure candidates where AI exposure may be real but hard to isolate; require backlog, vertical mix, and data-center customer evidence.
MOD is a thermal-management candidate for AI rack-density and data-center cooling demand; its survival test is data-center cooling revenue growth, customer wins, and liquid-cooling content.
CEG belongs in the AI power-supply reference lane; the key evidence gate is signed hyperscaler/data-center power agreements, regulatory approvals, and incremental economics from AI load growth.
Need primary-source market cap, revenue mix, backlog, customer concentration, and AI-specific order evidence for every underfollowed ticker before Layer 2 ranking.
Need ticker normalization and exchange validation for Taiwan-listed substrate names, including latest filings, English/Chinese investor materials, and monthly sales data.

Need market-pricing checks for all candidates: current market capitalization, EV/revenue, EV/EBITDA, analyst coverage, 3/6/12-month price moves, short interest where available, and whether AI exposure is already consensus.

AVGO should remain a reference anchor for custom AI accelerators and AI networking; use its growth/backlog/customer concentration to map upstream substrate, packaging, optical, and test bottlenecks rather than as an underfollowed candidate.

NVDA, TSM, ASML, ANET, MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, and META are high-attention reference anchors in this chunk; their primary Layer 2B role is to transmit demand signals into less-followed physical infrastructure nodes.

FLEX and JBL are underfollowed EMS hypotheses connected to AI server, rack, networking, and data-center hardware assembly, but they require primary-source proof of AI program materiality before ranking higher.

SMR is a speculative shadow candidate for long-duration AI power supply; it should not survive later Serenity layers without signed customer evidence, regulatory milestones, financing proof, and credible deployment timing.
Need primary-source market-cap, revenue mix, backlog/RPO, customer concentration, analyst coverage, and 3/6/12-month market-pricing checks for every ticker in this chunk.

Need direct source verification for FLEX and JBL AI exposure: latest 10-K/10-Q, earnings transcripts, investor decks, customer/program references, datacenter revenue materiality, and working-capital risk.

Need falsification triggers across this chunk: hyperscaler capex cuts, substrate lead-time compression, CoWoS capacity relief, margin pressure in AI networking, EMS inventory buildup, power interconnection delays, and failed SMR financing or licensing milestones.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. AI infrastructure should be mapped as a multi-bottleneck chain rather than a GPU-only chain. The current industry-chain pressure points cluster around advanced packaging/CoWoS capacity, ABF and IC substrates, HBM and memory backend capacity, optical interconnect/photonics, AI server power delivery, data-center electrical infrastructure, high-end passive components, inspection/metrology tools, and software-driven inference architecture shifts that keep CPU, networking, and memory demand sticky. Low-attention value may hide in substrate suppliers, packaging inspection tools, MLCC/passive components, medium-voltage switchgear, rack-level power semiconductors, and backend/test capacity rather than only in high-attention accelerator leaders.

supply_chain_map.node: AI demand: hyperscaler training and inference workloads
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The root demand driver is continued buildout of large-scale AI training clusters plus rapid growth in inference, especially custom-silicon inference at hyperscaler scale. This pulls demand through accelerators, CPUs, HBM, networking, power, cooling, optics, substrates, and data-center electrical systems.

supply_chain_map.node: AI accelerator and custom ASIC design
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-attention node that sets requirements for packaging, HBM, substrates, power delivery, and optical networking. It should be used as a demand anchor but not allowed to dominate the research map because many constraints sit one or two layers upstream.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced logic foundry capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Leading-edge process capacity remains strategically important for GPUs, AI ASICs, networking ASICs, and server CPUs, but in the current funnel it appears less hidden than packaging, substrates, power infrastructure, or passives.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging / CoWoS-like capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerators increasingly require advanced packaging to connect logic die, HBM stacks, interposers, and substrates. Cleanroom buildouts, tool acceptance, yield learning, and customer qualification make capacity additions slow and difficult to shortcut.

supply_chain_map.node: OSAT advanced packaging and test relief capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: When foundry-owned advanced packaging becomes constrained, OSATs can act as relief valves for assembly, test, and package-level engineering. Capacity, qualification, customer mix, and geographic expansion are key gating variables.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF substrates and high-end IC package substrates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-end AI chips require larger, more complex, higher-layer substrates with tighter tolerances. Supplier count is limited, qualification cycles are long, and access to ABF film allocation may reinforce incumbent substrate makers.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF film and substrate materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: ABF film is a critical material for advanced package substrates. If allocation is tight, new substrate entrants need not only capex and yield learning but also material access, making this a hidden upstream gate.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced PCB and ultra-HDI interconnect for AI servers and switches
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI servers, accelerator trays, high-speed switches, and rack-scale systems require higher-density, thermally managed boards. This is a second-order node often screened as generic PCB rather than AI infrastructure.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM memory supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: HBM is a well-known AI bottleneck because accelerator performance and package architecture depend on memory bandwidth. It also creates second-order effects in memory backend, testing, substrates, and packaging capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Memory backend packaging and test
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: HBM growth can crowd out other memory backend capacity and increase outsourcing needs. Lower-attention OSATs and memory test/packaging firms may become beneficiaries if utilization, pricing, and customer validation improve.

supply_chain_map.node: Inspection, metrology, and yield-control tools for packaging/substrates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As package body size, layer count, bump pitch, and substrate complexity increase, yield protection becomes more valuable. Inspection and metrology tool suppliers can be hidden chokepoints because they gate usable capacity rather than headline wafer starts.

supply_chain_map.node: Substrate and PCB process equipment: laser drilling, plating, chemistry, reflow
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Capacity additions for ABF substrates, HDI boards, and advanced packaging depend on specialized process tools. Tool lead times and qualification can create bottlenecks even before substrate capacity comes online.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical interconnects and AI datacenter transceivers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Larger AI clusters require high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnects between accelerators, switches, and racks. Optical modules, lasers, photodetectors, and related photonic components become scaling gates as networks move to higher speeds.

supply_chain_map.node: InP lasers, photodetectors, and compound semiconductor photonics
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Optical AI networks depend on constrained compound-semiconductor components. InP device capacity and qualification may be less visible than transceiver brands but can control the upstream availability of optical modules.

supply_chain_map.node: AI server high-end MLCCs and passive components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI servers require many high-performance capacitors to stabilize fast current draw from accelerators and high-power boards. The bottleneck is not commodity MLCCs, but small, high-capacitance, low-ESR/ESL products that only a few suppliers can mass-produce.

supply_chain_map.node: Rack-level power architecture: 48V/800V conversion, point-of-load, power modules
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI rack power density forces changes from grid input to point-of-load conversion. Suppliers with sockets across multiple conversion stages may benefit from integrated power-flow demand rather than isolated component demand.

supply_chain_map.node: Power semiconductors for AI racks
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI power delivery uses silicon, silicon carbide, gallium nitride, analog, and power-management components across the rack. This node can hide value in broad semiconductor companies not classified as AI accelerator suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center medium-voltage switchgear and electrical distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters require large power feeds, switchgear, transformers, breakers, and distribution hardware. Factory capacity and skilled labor constraints can stretch deployment timelines in months rather than days.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center cooling and thermal management
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-density AI racks increase liquid cooling, heat rejection, and facility-integration needs. This is a capacity-enabling node, though current provided evidence is stronger for electrical infrastructure than cooling.

supply_chain_map.node: Utility interconnection, grid capacity, and permitting
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Even if servers and chips are available, data-center deployment can be delayed by power availability, substation upgrades, interconnection queues, and permitting. This is a regulated-asset gate with low direct visibility in semiconductor narratives.

supply_chain_map.node: Server CPUs for agentic and CPU-heavy inference
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Inference architecture can keep server-class CPU demand sticky when workloads are not fully absorbed by accelerators. This complicates a simple GPU-only demand model and supports broader server platform demand.

supply_chain_map.node: AI networking ASICs, switches, and high-speed interconnect fabric
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Cluster scale requires fast east-west networking, switching, retimers, cables, optics, and custom silicon. Networking demand is increasingly tied to custom accelerators and inference buildouts.

supply_chain_map.node: Distribution, allocation, and customer prepayment/advance-payment gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Customer advances and capacity co-funding can reveal where buyers believe supply is not easily substitutable. Allocation behavior may identify hidden bottlenecks earlier than revenue recognition.

supply_chain_map.node: Certification, qualification, and tool acceptance gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Advanced packaging, substrates, optical components, and power systems require customer qualification, reliability testing, and tool acceptance cycles. These gates slow substitution and protect incumbent suppliers.

ticker_relationships.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify data-center computing revenue mix, AI server PCB content growth, margin contribution from HDI or advanced interconnect, customer concentration, backlog, and capex for ultra-HDI or substrate-like PCB.
ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Check TTMI latest 10-K, 10-Q, earnings call transcript, investor presentation, and segment disclosures for data-center, networking, high-density PCB, advanced interconnect, and AI-server references.
